govdocs-archive_org-zend-avesta-1st-volu:
The Zend-Avesta is the scripture of Zoroastrianism, among the oldest living religions on earth. Part I, the Vendidad, appears here in James Darmesteter's translation, in its revised second edition for the Sacred Books of the East.

The Vendidad is a law-book of purity and ritual. It teaches how to treat the dead, the earth, water, and fire, and how to fight the forces of pollution and evil in daily life. Darmesteter's English carried these laws to Western students of religion. As Part I of a world classic, it opens the series that the second volume continues.
modern-eloquence-vol-iii-after-dinner-sp:
Volume Three completes the after-dinner speeches in Thomas B. Reed's Modern Eloquence. Geo. L. Shuman and Company published it at Chicago, with copyright in 1903. Reed's associate editors were again Justin McCarthy, Rossiter Johnson, and Albert Ellery Bergh. This volume runs from speakers P through Z.

Its frontispiece is a photogravure of Priscilla and John Alden, the Puritan courtship New England orators loved to cite. A committee of selection chose the contents from the era's banquet circuit. Together the volumes form a library of occasional addresses, lectures, and toasts. They preserve how public men entertained and persuaded after dinner.
repertory-of-the-comedie-humaine-complet:
Cerfberr and Christophe compiled this repertory to Balzac's Comedie Humaine, a work the translator's preface notes was crowned by the French Academy. Its purpose, the preface says, is to list in alphabetical order every character in Balzac's society of novels. Each entry gives the chief points of that character's life.

Balzac made his people appear again and again across distinct novels, building a small world. Rastignac, for example, enters in Father Goriot as a law student and ends a minister and peer of France. The preface also explains choices on titles Balzac kept changing, such as Poor Relations, Lost Illusions, and the three parts of The Thirteen.
